screens.prompt: Both dates are serials, so put the number of days between the escalation and its resolution into D2.

hints.syntax: DAYS takes the end date first: =DAYS(C2,B2).
hints.func-days: Name DAYS rather than subtracting by hand, so the sheet says which date is the end.
hints.require-ref: Pass C2 and B2, so the second milestone fills down from the same pattern.
hints.value: 15 March minus 1 March is 14 days, with C2 as the end.
hints.error: #VALUE! means one of the two cells holds a date as text, so DAYS has no serial to subtract.

reject.why: subtracting in this order gives -14: a difference of days is not the same statement as DAYS
one date is not a distance — DAYS needs both ends
the serials typed in, so the next milestone has to be typed out again
the arguments are swapped, so the answer is -14
dividing by zero leaves #DIV/0! in the cell
the closing bracket is missing, so nothing runs

screens.prompt: Give the audit's length in whole weeks in D2, building the division on the days between the two dates.

hints.syntax: DAYS gives the days and /7 turns them into weeks: =DAYS(C2,B2)/7.
hints.func-days: Count the days first; the weeks are arithmetic on the result.
hints.require-ref: Read the start and end from B2 and C2 rather than typing the serials.
hints.value: 1 March to 3 May is 63 days, so 63/7 is 9 whole weeks.
hints.error: A negative week count means C2 and B2 are the wrong way round, since DAYS subtracts the second from the first.

reject.why: the right arithmetic without DAYS, so the row no longer says which date is the end
both ends are needed before anything can be divided into weeks
the dates typed in, so the answer stops following the row
the days, 63, before they are turned into weeks
the ends swapped, so the answer is -9 weeks
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
a stray closing bracket, so the formula will not parse

docs.explain:
DAYS takes an end date and a start date, in that order, and returns the distance between them in days. A plain subtraction C2-B2 answers the same question; naming the function makes the direction explicit. The result is an ordinary number, so arithmetic applies to it.

The first screen measures an escalation from 1 March to 15 March 2024 and expects 14. The second counts an audit from 1 March to 3 May, which is 63 days, then divides by seven for 9 weeks. Swap the arguments and DAYS returns -14 without an error.

A serial is only a date because the workbook counts from 1899, so 45352 means 1 March 2024 by convention. Keep a day count formatted as a number: format 14 as a date and the cell claims 14 January 1900.

errors.text: A date argument is text that Excel cannot read as a date, so there is no serial to subtract.
An argument sits outside the range of serials this workbook can hold, so no distance can be computed.
The arguments are the wrong way round, so DAYS returns -14 with no error to warn you.

seo.title: DAYS in Excel: date maths in days
seo.description: DAYS takes the end date first, so the answer is positive and the formula says which end is which. A date is a number, so weeks are that answer over seven.
